query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the heavy Ta constituent with the lighter Nb in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce its density without sacrificing its high strength and ductility at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr exhibiting a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ with high strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures (~1000 °C).
generation.intervention: Substitute Ta entirely (or nearly entirely) with Nb to form an equiatomic HfMoNbTiZr alloy.
generation.conditions: Mechanical and microstructural evaluation under standard loadings at room temperature and at an elevated temperature near 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic lattice will be modified by replacing heavy Ta atoms (density ~16.65 g/cm³) with lighter Nb atoms (density ~8.57 g/cm³), while retaining a similar BCC solid‐solution phase that provides solid-solution strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Nb has a lower atomic mass than Ta yet still offers a high melting point and good interaction with other elements. By replacing Ta with Nb, the alloy’s overall density decreases while maintaining the lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening mechanisms key to its mechanical performance at both room and high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The new HfMoNbTiZr alloy is expected to exhibit a lower overall density (with a significant reduction relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr) while maintaining comparable yield strength and ductility at room temperature and near 1000 °C. Some minor variations in absolute strength values may occur, but performance should remain within acceptable ranges for high-temperature applications.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with approximately 10.21 g/cm³ density and known high strength and ductility at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for conditions ranging from room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C under typical tensile and compressive loading regimes used in structural applications.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative changes in yield strength and ductility are uncertain until tested experimentally. There is also some uncertainty about how the modification might subtly affect high-temperature deformation mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare an equiatomic HfMoNbTiZr alloy via identical casting and homogenization procedures as used for HfMoTaTiZr. Perform identical mechanical tests (tensile/compressive tests) at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C, and measure the alloy density.
measurements: Density by Archimedes’ method or X-ray computed tomography
Yield strength and ultimate strength at room temperature using tension or compression tests
Yield strength and high-temperature strength (around 1000 °C) using high-temperature mechanical testing
Ductility metrics including elongation to failure at both temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HfMoNbTiZr alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant lower density compared to HfMoTaTiZr or if the yield strength and ductility at either room temperature or near 1000 °C drop by more than approximately 15% relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. Several theoretical models of solid-solution strengthening have been proposed to explain how different constituent elements affect room-temperature or elevated-temperature strength [,]. We previously designed a RHEA that exhibited higher elevated-temperature strength and discussed the effect of the constituent elements on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys by using the subtraction method []. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add elements such as Mo, which significantly interact with the other elements. For higher elevated-temperature strength, one should add the elements that possess a high melting point such as Mo, Nb, or Ta. For higher ductility, one should add more Nb. With Ti or Zr addition, both the elevated-temperature strength and the density decrease.

cited_evidence.text: We also calculated for MoNbTaVW with α = 2 and α = 16, and the σycal values were 1993 MPa and 2915 MPa. Then, we plot the lnσ of MoNbTaVW vs. T0.91 for T equals to 1200°C, 1400°C, and 1600°C. After linear fitting, the extrapolation method is used to estimate the strength at 298 K, which is 2950 MPa. Although 1993 MPa is not close to the 1246 MPa for room temperature strength of MoNbTaVW, 2915 MPa is almost consistent with 2950 MPa. Also, the temperature-strength curve of MoNbTaVW shows the plateau strength around 840 MPa and the Tc window around 600°C and 800°C, which means that there is a transition of slip mode. As a result, the room temperature strength of MoNbTaVW is controlled by screw dislocation, and the high temperature strength is controlled by edge dislocation. We believe that this mechanism can comprehensively explain the Tc, plateau strength phenomena and high elevated-temperature strength that occurs in bcc-type RHEAs.
